title: India's Dead Sailors Have Put Modi in a Corner. He Meets Trump at the G7 Next Week.
excerpt: Three seafarers killed, three ships struck in one week. Unions want answers. The opposition smells blood. And the G7 summit is days away.
body:
India's Dead Sailors Have Put Modi in a Corner. He Meets Trump at the G7 Next Week.

India's 300,000-strong merchant marine workforce has become collateral damage in America's three-month-old war with Iran, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi now faces a politically agonising question: how do you condemn a military ally for killing your citizens — days before you sit across from that ally at the G7?

The fury erupted after the US military struck three Indian-crewed tankers in a single week. On Wednesday, precision munitions slammed into the engine room of the Palau-flagged tanker Settebello off Oman. Twenty-one Indian sailors were rescued by the Omani Navy. Three were found dead — the first merchant seafarers confirmed killed since Washington began its naval blockade of Iranian ports on April 13.

A day later, two Hellfire missiles hit the engine room of the Guinea-Bissau-flagged Jalveer. All twenty crew members survived. On Monday, the Marivex had been disabled in a similar operation. In each case, the US military said the crews had "repeatedly failed to comply with directions from American forces."

'These Attacks Must Stop'

New Delhi summoned Jason Meeks, the US charge d'affaires, to deliver a formal demarche — a rare diplomatic escalation between two countries that have been deepening their strategic partnership for more than a decade.

"The attacks that are happening must stop," foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told reporters on Thursday. "We call for dialogue and diplomacy so that we can have an early return to peace and stability in the region."

Shipping Minister Sarbananda Sonowal called the deaths a "profound loss to our maritime family" and confirmed the remains of the three sailors would be repatriated along with the survivors. The Directorate General of Shipping issued an advisory urging all Indian seafarers in conflict-affected waters to exercise "the highest degree of caution." This advisory resonates deeply with the Indian diaspora, many of whom have family members working in maritime professions, highlighting the personal stakes involved.

Domestic Pressure Mounts

India's opposition seized on the crisis. The Indian National Congress said Modi "cannot evade responsibility when that relationship fails to protect Indian lives," pointing directly at the Prime Minister's much-publicised personal rapport with Trump.

The Centre of Indian Trade Unions went further: "When a foreign military kills Indian workers in international waters, the government of India must speak — loudly and firmly."

The families of the dead sailors are demanding answers. Rajesh Sharma, father of one of the three men killed, told news agency ANI: "I have only one demand — that my son's remains be brought back. I want to know what happened in his last moments."

Shivanand Chaurasia, another of the deceased, had gone to sea nine months ago and told his father earlier in the week that everything was fine.

The Forward Seamen's Union of India says the strikes have triggered "panic and fear" among Indian seafarers, many of whom remain stranded in the Gulf. It questioned why US forces needed to fire on a commercial vessel carrying no ammunition when they "could easily board the ship and detain it." This fear is echoed by many in the diaspora, as they worry about the safety of their loved ones at sea and the implications for remittances that support families back home.

The G7 Complication

Modi is expected to meet Trump on the sidelines of the G7 leaders' summit in France next week. What was meant to be a discussion about trade, technology, and the broader Indo-Pacific partnership now carries the weight of three dead sailors and a domestic electorate watching closely.

The timing is particularly delicate because Trump simultaneously claims a deal with Iran is imminent — a deal that, if real, would make the very blockade that killed these sailors unnecessary within days. On Thursday evening, he called off planned strikes on Iran and said the Strait of Hormuz would "officially open as soon as we sign."

For Trump, the politics are equally uncomfortable. The blockade has been a domestic headache, with rising gasoline prices and sinking approval ratings. Some Republicans have openly worried that the war's unpopularity could cost them control of Congress in November.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

India supplies the world's largest contingent of merchant marine labour. Many Indian-Americans have family members working on commercial vessels in the Gulf, and the crisis has raised concerns about their safety and well-being. The emotional toll on families abroad is significant, as they grapple with uncertainty and fear for their loved ones.

The crisis also underlines a structural geopolitical tension: India needs American security cooperation in the Indo-Pacific but cannot appear to acquiesce when its citizens are killed by American weapons. The diaspora is closely monitoring how Modi addresses these issues, as it could impact their ties to India and their sense of security in their professional lives.

How Modi navigates this at the G7 will signal whether the US-India relationship can survive the pressures of a real war — one that India did not start, does not want, but whose consequences are now washing up on its shores.
